notes.title: Start here: one small fix studied in depth
notes.body:
master1 is a NestJS employer-of-record monorepo (the same GlobalWork codebase studied in another quest). This pack is about its `astraupskill/` course, which takes one real bug fix in `apps/api/src/modules/tasks/tasks.service.ts` and studies it from every side: the request path, the concept behind it, the diff, the tests and a trace lab.

Read in this order:

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: `PATCH /api/tasks/:id` from the global pipe to the service, line by line.
2. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: why a status value is not the same as an event time.
3. `astraupskill/03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: the one-hunk diff and why it has that shape.
4. `astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: what the focused tests control and assert.
5. `astraupskill/07-TRACE-LAB.md`: fill in the table yourself before reading its answers.

Keep `TasksService.update` (lines 51-80) open the whole time. It is short; most quizzes are about which keys it puts into the update payload.

notes.title: Reading TasksService.update key by key
notes.body:
`update` loads the row as `before`, then builds the `data` object from four conditional spreads, one per optional DTO field. For each spread, note two things:

- **Which test opens it.** Some use a truthiness check (`dto.x ? ... : {}`), others a presence check (`dto.x !== undefined ? ... : {}`). Work out which inputs (missing, `null`, `""`, a real value) open each one.
- **What it writes.** For the status spread, list the possible `completedAt` values and the condition that chooses each.

Then read the rest of the method: what the audit call records in `before` and `after`, whether it runs on every request, and whether the update and the audit share a transaction.

Also read `main.ts` lines 17-23 and `dto/update-task.dto.ts`: the global `ValidationPipe` options and the decorators decide what can reach the service at all, including how `@IsOptional()` treats `null`.

notes.title: How the focused tests work, and what a race looks like
notes.body:
`tests/tasks-service-completion.test.mjs` loads the real service source into a Node `vm` context through `tests/helpers/load-typescript.mjs`, with stubs for Prisma and audit and a fixed clock. Read the three tests and, for each, write down what it would catch if someone broke the completion logic in a different way. Note how the third test compares the payload, and read the "cross-realm gotcha" section for why.

Then do trace 3 in the trace lab on paper: two lanes, two writers, one read at line 52 and one write at line 53. Mark the gap between them, and decide what each writer's `before` says when it reaches its write. Compare with the "Limits worth naming" list in the concepts page.

Finally, note what the suite cannot prove; the testing page lists it.

# Trace state, event time and audit separately

notes.title: A repeat DONE keeps its history
notes.body:
The status spread runs because `dto.status` is "DONE". Inside it, `completedAt` is `before.status === "DONE" ? before.completedAt : new Date()`, and the task was already DONE, so Monday 09:00 is written back. Priority is updated by its own spread.

- *Tuesday's save time* is exactly the original bug: the old code looked only at the requested status.
- *null* is the value for leaving DONE, not for repeating it.
- *No completedAt key*: the status spread runs whenever a status is supplied, so the key is present.

notes.title: Reusing the old value reuses null too
notes.body:
For a repeat DONE the code writes `before.completedAt` without looking at it. This legacy row holds null, so the update data carries `completedAt: null` and the row stays as it was. The concepts page calls this deliberate: preserving the value does not invent a history, and repairing such rows is a separate data decision.

- *Backfilled current time* would invent a completion that did not happen at that moment.
- *createdAt* and *updatedAt* are never read by this code path.

notes.title: Any other status clears the timestamp
notes.body:
"OPEN" is supplied, so the status spread runs and writes `status: "OPEN"`. The ternary `dto.status === "DONE" ? ... : null` takes its else branch, so `completedAt: null` is written. That is the product convention for leaving DONE.

- *Kept as T1* would leave a completion time on an open task.
- *No completedAt key*: the key is always present when a status is supplied.
- *Set to now* happens only when entering DONE.

notes.title: No status, no completion keys, still an audit row
notes.body:
With only `priority` in the body, the status spread contributes `{}`, the assignee and due-date spreads see `undefined` and contribute nothing, and line 64 adds `priority`. So `data` is exactly `{ priority: "HIGH" }`. The audit call after the update has no condition, so a task.updated row is written every time.

- *completedAt: null too* is the unintended write that test 3 guards against.
- *status and completedAt as well*: they appear only when a status is sent.
- *No audit row*: the audit runs whether or not status changed.

notes.title: A falsy status skips the branch
notes.body:
`@IsOptional()` skips validation for `null`, so `{ "status": null }` reaches the service. There, `dto.status ? ... : {}` treats null as falsy and contributes nothing: no `status`, no `completedAt`. The update still runs (with empty data) and the audit row is still written.

- *Prisma rejects it with a 500* is what would happen if the check were "tidied" to `!== undefined`; the worked change warns against that.
- *Becomes OPEN*: nothing maps null to a status.
- *400 from the DTO*: `@IsOptional()` lets null through.

notes.title: A presence check plus || null
notes.body:
Line 65 is `dto.assigneeId !== undefined ? { assigneeId: dto.assigneeId || null } : {}`. An empty string is defined, so the branch runs, and `"" || null` is null. The task is unassigned. `@IsString()` accepts the empty string, so validation does not stop it.

- *No key because "" is falsy*: that would be a truthiness check; this one is a presence check.
- *Stored as ""*: the `|| null` converts it.
- *400*: an empty string is still a string.

notes.title: Unknown keys never reach the service
notes.body:
`main.ts` installs `new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true })`. `completedAt` is not declared on `UpdateTaskDto`, and `forbidNonWhitelisted` turns an unknown property into a 400 before the controller runs. A client cannot set the timestamp directly.

- *Stripped silently*: that is `whitelist` alone; `forbidNonWhitelisted` rejects instead.
- *Backdated to 2020*: the service never sees the key.
- *Logged in the audit*: the request fails before the service.

notes.title: A stale before decides the write
notes.body:
Writer A read OPEN at line 52. When it resumes, its `before.status` is still OPEN, so the ternary takes the "entering DONE" path and writes `new Date()`, T2, over B's T1. The update's `where` is only `{ id }` and there is no version or status predicate, so nothing notices.

- *T1 as a repeat*: that needs A's `before` to say DONE, and it was read before B committed.
- *null*: nothing clears the time when both write DONE.
- *Prisma rejects the stale update*: without a predicate on status or version, the update matches the row and succeeds.

excerpts.quote: const before = await this.prisma.task.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { id } });

notes.title: The audit row records status and priority only
notes.body:
The audit call passes `before: { status: before.status, priority: before.priority }` and `after: { status: task.status, priority: task.priority }`. A dueAt-only edit therefore produces a row whose before and after look identical: the field that changed is not recorded at all.

- *Only dueAt*: the payload is fixed to status and priority.
- *status, priority and dueAt*: dueAt is never included.
- *Every column*: the audit receives two small objects, not the rows.

notes.title: Two awaited calls, no transaction
notes.body:
`update` awaits `prisma.task.update(...)`, then awaits `this.audit.log(...)` as a separate call. Neither is inside `prisma.$transaction`, so when the audit insert throws, the task change has already been committed and stays. The codebase map points out that other services (expenses, for example) do use transactions.

- *Both rolled back*: there is no surrounding transaction to roll back.
- *Retried*: nothing retries the audit or the update.
- *Compensating update*: no undo logic exists.

notes.title: Different realms, different prototypes
notes.body:
The service is evaluated inside a `vm` context, so every object it creates has that context's `Object.prototype`. `assert.deepEqual` notices the prototype mismatch and fails with "same structure but are not reference-equal". `Object.keys(data)` returns an array built in the test's own realm, so comparing it works and still checks exactly which keys were sent.

- *A Prisma proxy*: Prisma is a stub here; `data` is a plain object from the service.
- *Date by reference*: test 3 has no Date in its payload.
- *The audit double mutates data*: it only records its own argument.

notes.title: Test 2 pins first completion
notes.body:
Test 2's first half moves a task from IN_PROGRESS, whose `completedAt` is null, to DONE and expects the fixed clock instant. A fix that always reuses `before.completedAt` writes null there, and the assertion's `getTime()` call on null throws. The testing page names this exactly.

- *Test 1* expects the old value on a repeat DONE, which the "always reuse" version still writes.
- *Test 3* sends only priority; the status branch never runs.
- *None*: the first half of test 2 fails.
